title: Nipah Virus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Nipah virus (NiV) infection is an emerging zoonotic disease caused by a highly pathogenic Henipavirus that can cause severe encephalitis and acute respiratory illness, with high case fatality rates. Transmission occurs through exposure to infected bats or intermediate hosts, consumption of contaminated foods (eg, raw date palm sap), or close contact with infected individuals and their body fluids. Clinical presentation typically begins with nonspecific febrile symptoms that can progress rapidly to altered mental status, seizures, coma, and respiratory distress, with multiorgan dysfunction in severe cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion supported by epidemiologic risk factors and laboratory confirmation, most commonly with real-time reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction from respiratory samples, blood, urine, or cerebrospinal fluid. Management is primarily supportive and requires strict infection prevention and control practices to limit human-to-human transmission, alongside timely public health notification to facilitate contact tracing and community-level mitigation.

title: Nipah Virus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Course participants learn to recognize the clinical spectrum of NiV infection, identify exposures and outbreak-related risk factors that increase pretest probability, and apply appropriate diagnostic strategies to confirm infection while differentiating NiV from other causes of encephalitis and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Participants also learn to implement isolation precautions, coordinate escalation of supportive care for neurologic and respiratory complications, and integrate public health actions such as reporting, contact tracing, and quarantine when indicated. Collaboration within an interprofessional team enhances outcomes by aligning early neurologic assessment, critical care support, infection control practices, and pharmacy input to consider investigational or regionally recommended therapies, while also supporting rehabilitation and mental health needs during recovery. Coordinated communication among clinicians, nursing staff, infection prevention specialists, laboratory staff, and veterinary and biosecurity stakeholders strengthens surveillance and reduces spillover and transmission risk at human-animal interfaces.

title: Nipah Virus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify epidemiologic risk factors and exposure pathways for Nipah virus infection to guide timely clinical suspicion and appropriate triage. Differentiate Nipah virus infection from alternative infectious and noninfectious causes of encephalitis and severe respiratory disease using clinical findings and outbreak context. Select appropriate diagnostic tests and specimens based on timing from symptom onset, cross-reactivity, and biosafety constraints. title: Nipah Virus -- Introduction
content: Nipah virus (NiV) is an RNA virus belonging to the family Paramyxoviridae and the genus Henipavirus , which also includes Hendra virus , Langya virus , Mojiang virus , and Cedar virus . The NiV was first identified in Malaysia in 1998 and has since caused numerous outbreaks in and around South and Southeast Asia. The NiV is a World Health Organization (WHO) priority pathogen due to its propensity for causing outbreaks. [1]

title: Nipah Virus -- Introduction
content: The NiV is a zoonotic disease, and the reservoir is the Pteropus fruit bat. Spillover likely occurred in pigs and subsequently in humans. The NiV is considered a biological safety level 4 pathogen because no effective treatment or vaccine is available. [2] Because NiV is a zoonotic disease, a One Health approach involving humans, animals, and the environment is necessary to prevent further spillovers.

title: Nipah Virus -- Etiology
content: NiV belongs to the Henipavirus genus, the Orthoparamyxovirinae subfamily, and the Paramyxoviridae family. NiV is a negative-sense, single-stranded, enveloped RNA virus, composed of 6 genes, including nucleocapsid (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix (M), and large polymerase (L) genes, which make up the ribonucleoprotein and facilitate viral budding. NiV also encodes fusion (F) and attachment glycoproteins (G) that mediate host cell attachment and subsequent entry, as well as facilitating neutralization by antibodies. [3] This G protein binds to ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 host receptors on a wide range of endothelial and neuronal cells, allowing the virus to infect many mammalian species, including the reservoir host, the Pteropus fruit bat. However, NiV has been known to infect rodents, weasels, and various monkey species. [2]

title: Nipah Virus -- Epidemiology
content: Transmission of the NiV can occur through direct contact with infected animals (bats, pigs, or horses) or their body fluids (blood, urine, or saliva), ingestion of contaminated food products (palm sap or fruit), or close contact with an infected person or their body fluids (nasal or respiratory droplets, aerosols, urine, or blood). Human-to-human transmission has been documented, including during a 2023 outbreak in Kerala, India. [4] Transmission appears to exhibit seasonal variation, with an increased incidence from December to May in South Asia (although cases have been reported as late as July), typically associated with harvesting raw date palm sap. [5] In Southeast Asia, NiV incidence is typically nonseasonal and has been linked to intensive pig farming in Malaysia and Singapore. [6] [7] The virus remains viable for days on fruit pulp and palm sap, prolonging the potential duration of human exposure. [8] [9] Additionally, NiV has a half-life of 18 hours in bat urine. [10] After exposure, the incubation period ranges from 4 to 14 days. [6]

title: Nipah Virus -- Epidemiology
content: Two distinct strains of NiV are described: the Bangladesh and Malaysian strains. [11] Of these, South Asian strains have a greater propensity for human-to-human transmission. [12] The first recognized outbreak of NiV infection was reported near the city of Ipoh in Perak, Malaysia, in 1998. [2] In March 1999, NiV was isolated for the first time from a patient’s cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in Sungai Nipah village, from which the virus derives its name. [1] In 1999, another outbreak involving 11 cases and one death occurred in Singapore. [13]

title: Nipah Virus -- Epidemiology
content: In Bangladesh, the epidemiology of NiV differed, starting with an outbreak of encephalitis in Meherpur in 2001. Notably, pigs were not implicated as a vector because pig farming was not practiced in Bangladesh, a predominantly Muslim country. Subsequently, multiple seasonal outbreaks have occurred, each likely representing a separate spillover event. [2]

title: Nipah Virus -- Epidemiology
content: In 2001, an outbreak of encephalitis was reported in Siliguri, West Bengal, India, which is geographically adjacent to Bangladesh. In retrospect, this outbreak was likely caused by the NiV. [14] Therefore, in Bangladesh and during the Siliguri outbreak, the consumption of fresh date palm sap is thought to have caused a direct spillover of NiV from bats to humans. [15] Moreover, in 2014, an outbreak was reported in the Philippines, in which NiV transmission occurred via exposure to infected horses, similar to that observed with Hendra virus infections in Australia. [2] [16] Between 2018 and 2025, the southern Indian state of Kerala reported 8 distinct NiV outbreaks, in which fruit bats were once again implicated in spillover events. [17] [18] [19]

title: Nipah Virus -- Pathophysiology
content: Flying foxes ( Pteropus giganteus) are the reservoir hosts of the NiV in Bangladesh and India. [20] [21] Furthermore, Pteropus species of bats in other countries (Cambodia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Madagascar) have anti-NiV antibodies. [22] [23] [24] [25] Rarely, other  bat species can be reservoir hosts. [23] [26] [27] Pigs served as intermediate hosts of the Nipah virus during the initial outbreak in Malaysia and Singapore, and horses served as intermediate hosts during the outbreak in the Philippines. [28]

title: Nipah Virus -- Pathophysiology
content: NiV enters humans and other hosts via the oronasal route. High concentrations of antigen in lymphoid and respiratory tissue suggest that these are the probable sites of initial replication. The NiV attachment glycoprotein plays a critical role in viral transmission using the human receptors ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3. [29] NiV infects respiratory tract epithelium and induces inflammatory cytokines, leading to a disease similar to acute respiratory distress syndrome. [30] The kidneys, spleen, and brain may be involved, leading to multiorgan failure. [10]

title: Nipah Virus -- History and Physical
content: Initial symptoms are fever, headache, dizziness, and vomiting. Affected individuals may also develop respiratory tract involvement. The clinical features of the Malaysian and Indian variants of NiV differ: respiratory illness is reported in patients from India and Bangladesh, whereas significant respiratory involvement is usually not present in patients in Malaysia. [14] However, serosurveys have established asymptomatic infection in 8% to 45% of NiV cases, revealing the spectrum of disease. [6] [31] This initial presentation is followed by rapidly progressive encephalitis resulting in lethargy, disorientation, and coma. Central nervous system (CNS) symptoms include decreased level of consciousness, brainstem dysfunction, myoclonus, areflexia, hypotonia, and cerebellar signs. Clinical deterioration is signified by hypertension, worsening level of consciousness, and tachycardia. [7] In fulminant illness, multiorgan dysfunction, gastrointestinal tract bleeding, and renal failure may occur.

title: Nipah Virus -- History and Physical
content: In Bangladesh outbreaks, up to 69% of patients had respiratory tract symptoms, and some had acute respiratory distress syndrome. [6] [32] [33] [34] Patients may also have long-term neurologic complications from encephalitis, including fatigue, ocular motor palsies, cervical dystonia, focal weakness, and facial paralysis. In a small proportion of patients, the onset of the illness may be delayed, and there may be relapses after recovery from the acute infection. [35]

title: Nipah Virus -- Evaluation
content: Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hyponatremia, and elevated alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase levels are commonly observed. [13] NiV can be detected in urine, blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and respiratory secretions by culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Real-time reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) remains the most widely used and useful test. [36] [37] [38] [39] [40] Serology is typically a first-line investigation for NIV; however, it is not specific without serum neutralization in a biosafety level 4 laboratory, or PCR confirmation, because IgM can often cross-react with related species (such as Hendra ). At symptom onset, IgM sensitivity may be as low as 44% to 50%, increasing to 60% to 71% by day 4 and 100% by day 12. [41] The NiV IgG positivity may be as low as 7% in the first week of symptoms, then increase over time, with seroconversion. IgG testing is mostly useful for epidemiologic studies, such as serosurveys, to estimate the population burden of NiV. [42] No lateral flow rapid diagnostic assays are currently available for NiV.

title: Nipah Virus -- Evaluation
content: In most patients infected with NiV, CSF analysis shows an elevated white blood cell count or protein level. [6] In acute NiV infection, virus-specific antibodies were present in the serum in more than 70% of samples but in less than one-third of CSF samples. The presence of the virus in CSF culture was strongly associated with increased mortality. [43]

title: Nipah Virus -- Evaluation
content: Electroencephalography in encephalitis can show bilateral temporal periodic complexes of diffuse, symmetric, sharp and slow waves occurring every 1 to 2 seconds. [44] Electroencephalographic slowing correlates with the severity of NiV encephalitis. Although electroencephalography is sensitive for detecting findings suggestive of NiV, it is not diagnostic for NiV infection due to low specificity.[Kong et al. Neurol J Southeast Asia . 1999] Typical MRI findings include multiple 2- to 7-mm lesions, best visualized on T2-weighted images, in the subcortical and deep white matter of the cerebral hemispheres, periventricular areas, and the corpus callosum, without associated cerebral edema or mass effect. A minority of patients demonstrate leptomeningeal or parenchymal lesion enhancement on MRI. [6] [45] [46]

title: Nipah Virus -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with NiV infection should be isolated, and infection control measures should be implemented. Treatment is primarily supportive. Ribavirin is an antiviral agent effective against other paramyxoviruses, such as the Human respiratory syncytial virus . Reports on its efficacy are unclear, with conflicting evidence: some human studies show reduced mortality, while animal models show no benefit. [47] [48] However, the National Centre for Disease Control in India recommends ribavirin for NiV infection. [6] [47] Ribavirin has also been used on a compassionate basis in the Kerala outbreaks. [49] Acyclovir, remdesivir, and chloroquine are other drugs under review as potential therapeutic options, but supporting data are currently limited. [13] [48] [50] Exploratory research into preventative vaccines is ongoing, including the use of mRNA technology to stimulate protective antibody responses. [51]

title: Nipah Virus -- Treatment / Management
content: Favipiravir, which is licensed for the treatment of influenza in Japan, has demonstrated efficacy in hamsters, but human data are lacking. [52] A human monoclonal antibody, m102.4 (directed against the Hendra virus glycoprotein), has shown promise in early trials, with compassionate use for both treatment and postexposure prophylaxis in NiV infection during the Kerala outbreak. This treatment is currently undergoing phase 1 clinical trials in Australia. [49] Patients should be discharged only after a negative RT-PCR test result from a throat swab. Patients remain in isolation for 21 days following confirmation of the infection. [1]

title: Nipah Virus -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis includes any disease presenting with fever and encephalitis or acute respiratory distress syndrome; however, epidemiology (travel history, exposure, and ongoing outbreaks) helps clarify the diagnosis. The differential diagnosis of NiV infection includes: [53] Japanese encephalitis virus West Nile virus encephalitis Measles virus encephalitis (subacute sclerosing panencephalitis) Other Henipavirus infections Autoimmune encephalitis Rabies virus infection Dengue virus encephalitis Cerebral malaria Scrub typhus Leptospirosis Human herpesvirus encephalitis Bacterial meningitis

title: Nipah Virus -- Prognosis
content: The case fatality rates range from 40% to 100%. Poor prognostic factors include older age and severe brainstem involvement. [53] Brainstem involvement may manifest as abnormal oculocephalic reflexes and tachycardia. [6] Biochemically, viral isolation from CSF is associated with a poorer prognosis and increased mortality. [43] On an electroencephalogram, bitemporal periodic complexes are commonly seen in comatose and deceased encephalitis cases.[Kong et al. Neurol J Southeast Asia . 1999] Prognosis and case fatality rates also depend on the strain of the virus, with the Malaysian variant demonstrating lower rates. [54]

title: Nipah Virus -- Prognosis
content: Infection with NiV is associated with relapsed and late-onset encephalitis, which can manifest months to years after the initial infection and may present with neurologic signs, fevers, headaches, and seizures. [55] A relapse may be characterized on imaging by progressive changes from focal hyperperfusion to hypoperfusion on CT positron-emission tomography. Brain imaging with MRI may show confluent cortical involvement, in contrast to the focal hyperintense changes seen in acute NiV encephalitis, and may show less brainstem involvement. [45] Relapsed and late-onset NiV encephalitis is typically associated with a lower mortality than acute encephalitis (approximately 18%). [55] Triggers for relapsed and late-onset encephalitis are still being investigated, but autopsy results indicate greater viral inclusions and larger parenchymal lesions in relapsed disease than in acute encephalitis. Relapsed disease is also associated with the persistence of viral antigens despite the absence of the virus, suggesting a pathogen-host interaction rather than direct viral cytopathic effects.

title: Nipah Virus -- Complications
content: Patients may have residual neurological deficits, including behavioral changes, cervical dystonia, cerebellar dysfunction, oculomotor palsies, weakness, and facial paralysis. [56] These manifestations may persist for months to years after the infection, resulting in long-term functional impairment and significant impacts on quality of life. Results from one study reported that 10 years after NiV infection, a small proportion of patients had persisting fatigue, daytime somnolence, and ongoing focal neurological deficits, resulting in functional impairment on the Modified Rankin Scale.[Siva SR et al. Neurology Asia . 2009] [35]

title: Nipah Virus -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education is critical in disease prevention, especially given the lack of effective treatment. Patient education should focus on preventing contamination or consumption of raw date palm sap and reducing exposure to infected wildlife. The WHO also recommends avoiding exposure to bats and pigs when an outbreak is suspected, and to fruit bitten by bats or raw date palm sap.[WHO. Nipah Virus . 2018] Protective clothing is recommended for people involved in the slaughter of animals. Facilities suspected of having an NiV outbreak should be immediately quarantined, and local veterinary and agricultural authorities notified to implement environmental controls. Virus containment may include culling infected animals and disposing of dead carcasses by burial or incineration. Because NiV is a reportable disease in the United States and in many Asian countries where NiV is endemic, public health authorities should also be immediately notified of any suspected or confirmed NiV human cases to institute isolation and restriction measures in exposed communities. Human-to-human transmission during an outbreak can be contained by limiting exposure through preventive health measures and the use of personal protective equipment. Contact tracing and quarantine of potential contacts form a large part of outbreak response. [1] [18] [57]
contents: Nipah Virus -- Deterrence and Patient Education. Patient education is critical in disease prevention, especially given the lack of effective treatment. Patient education should focus on preventing contamination or consumption of raw date palm sap and reducing exposure to infected wildlife. The WHO also recommends avoiding exposure to bats and pigs when an outbreak is suspected, and to fruit bitten by bats or raw date palm sap.[WHO. Nipah Virus . 2018] Protective clothing is recommended for people involved in the slaughter of animals. Facilities suspected of having an NiV outbreak should be immediately quarantined, and local veterinary and agricultural authorities notified to implement environmental controls. Virus containment may include culling infected animals and disposing of dead carcasses by burial or incineration. Because NiV is a reportable disease in the United States and in many Asian countries where NiV is endemic, public health authorities should also be immediately notified of any suspected or confirmed NiV human cases to institute isolation and restriction measures in exposed communities. Human-to-human transmission during an outbreak can be contained by limiting exposure through preventive health measures and the use of personal protective equipment. Contact tracing and quarantine of potential contacts form a large part of outbreak response. [1] [18] [57]

title: Nipah Virus -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Nipah virus infection is a potentially highly lethal disease that requires immediate public health notification to prevent transmission to susceptible individuals in high-risk animal-handling occupations and to close contacts of those infected. Diagnosis may require RT-PCR in the clinical context of encephalitis, a febrile illness with focal neurological deficits, or an acute respiratory distress syndrome. Nipah virus has pandemic potential, and further research is warranted into its epidemiology and therapeutic options, given its priority pathogen status with the WHO.

title: Nipah Virus -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The management of NiV infection is best accomplished through an interprofessional team approach that includes infectious disease specialists, clinicians, and nursing staff, as well as engagement with external stakeholders in the veterinary and biosecurity fields. Early involvement of a neurologist will be needed to exclude other neurological diseases that present with encephalitis. Management is mainly supportive as the infection has no cure, and treatment options are otherwise limited. Pharmacists and pharmacologists may need to be consulted to consider the use of ribavirin in some individuals. Ongoing consultations with numerous specialists (such as psychiatrists) and allied health professionals may be required, depending on symptomatology and ongoing functional impairment from neuropsychiatric deficits following recovery from acute infection. Since no effective treatment exists, preventative measures from an interdisciplinary team are critical. This includes engagement with public health and infection control experts to prevent human-to-human transmission.
